business: Gaines & Associates, PC (formerly Gaines, Goldenfarb & Associates) - CPA firm, 105 Fieldcrest Ave, Suite 501, Edison, NJ 08837
opportunity: Pre-close assistant for client books: match transactions, queue exceptions with proposed fixes, draft adjusting journal entries, chase missing documents, assemble the close pack - with a reviewer approving every posting

problem.summary: The firm sells payroll, AP/AR, bank and card reconciliations and month-end closings as ongoing outsourced services, and is hiring a Senior Accounting Manager whose duty is to own month-end close and reporting for multiple clients at once. If each client sits on a different stack, the same reconcile-review-chase-approve sequence is re-performed per client with no single standardized pipeline, and the work is sold as recurring manual service rather than software. Only part of that stack can be verified: the firm's own site confirms QuickBooks as an anchor accounting product line, while the wider list (Bill.com, NetSuite, CCH ProSystem fx, Reach Reporting, Power BI/Tableau, HubSpot) comes from the firm's Senior Accounting Manager posting, whose body could not be re-opened during this revision, and search descriptions quoting that posting disagree about which tools are required versus 'nice to have'. The client stack is therefore a discovery question, not a confirmed fact. Files move through a third-party secure link (ProtectedXchange) in the site header, with no task list or automated document chasing attached to it. The cost is capacity the firm must hire for instead of billing for: the audit puts the recoverable time at roughly 225-720 staff hours a year, about $13,600-$43,600 at the BLS New Jersey accountant benchmark. That figure rests on assumptions the firm has not confirmed (25-40 books a month, 1.5-3 hours per close, 50% handover), so the pilot must measure the real baseline first.

solution.design: A per-client pre-close pipeline that runs on a close calendar (T-7, T-5, T-1 before each client's close date) and on new bank/AP activity. For each client book it: pulls the trial balance, bank/card transactions and open bills; auto-matches at the transaction level with deterministic rules first (amount, date tolerance, vendor alias, recurring pattern) and an LLM only for the residue (fuzzy descriptions, split transactions, ambiguous vendors); ranks every unmatched item into an exception queue carrying a proposed resolution, the GL account, a confidence score and the supporting document; drafts adjusting journal entries with GL code and backup attached; sends missing-document requests in the reviewer's name with a tracked thread and a reminder schedule; and at the end assembles the close pack (P&L, balance sheet, KPI deltas versus prior month, open exceptions list). Nothing is written to the client ledger until a named reviewer approves the line item in the queue, and approved entries post with an idempotency key so a retry cannot double-post. Build rather than buy because no published product combines per-client reconciliation logic with the firm's own review standard and checklist, but buy or borrow the commodity parts: Intuit's own MIT-licensed QuickBooks Online MCP server for the QBO surface (29 entity types, JournalEntry and Attachable CRUD, QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE/UPDATE/DELETE flags), an open-source document parser, and a hosted transactional email API. The AP layer (BILL v3) and any NetSuite/CCH ProSystem access are conditional: they are wired only if discovery confirms a pilot book actually uses them. Keep the runtime in a US region under the firm's control, one database schema per client with hard tenant isolation, and a full audit log of every read, proposal, approval and post.

solution.human_in_the_loop: A named reviewer (the Senior Accounting Manager or a senior on the book) is the only actor that can move an item from 'proposed' to 'posted'. Controls: (1) every proposed journal entry carries the GL account, the source transactions and the confidence score, and posts only on explicit approval of that line; (2) anything above a firm-set dollar threshold, in a flagged account, or below a confidence floor is escalated with no proposal attached; (3) posting uses an idempotency key and a one-click reversal, and the run log shows who approved what and when; (4) outbound document-chase emails are generated by the agent but the first two weeks are reviewed before send, and reminders are capped so a client is never spammed; (5) a weekly exception digest goes to the manager listing anything unresolved or auto-matched with low confidence; (6) a hard kill switch suppresses the QBO write tools via the MCP server's QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE flag. The firm remains the decision-maker on every number that reaches a client's ledger.

pilot.scope: 3 client books on QuickBooks Online, two consecutive monthly closes; BILL is added only if discovery confirms a chosen book uses it. In scope: read-only ingestion first, then the exception queue with proposed resolutions and draft journal entries, tracked document-chase emails, and the assembled close pack. Out of scope: NetSuite and CCH ProSystem clients, payroll filings, tax-return work, any autonomous posting, and any change to ProtectedXchange or the client portal. Pricing, invoicing and client communication stay entirely with the firm.
pilot.weeks: 4 weeks elapsed (two monthly closes), after roughly 2 weeks of build
success_metrics: Reviewer minutes per book per close, measured against the baseline for the same 3 books (target: at least 30% lower by the second pilot close)
Share of transactions cleared without reviewer touch (target: 60%+ by close two, reported separately for deterministic vs model-assisted matches)
Acceptance rate of proposed journal entries (target: 80%+ accepted or accepted-with-edit; a low rate means the proposals are noise)
Zero entries posted without an approval record, and zero postings that had to be reversed for error
Share of missing-document requests sent within one business day of detection (target: 95%)
Both pilot closes completed by the firm's normal due date, with the pack produced from the agent run rather than rebuilt by hand
pilot.baseline_method: Before any build, have the reviewer keep a simple per-book, per-close time log for the two most recent closes: minutes on reconciliation, minutes on exception chasing, minutes drafting entries, minutes assembling the pack - plus the count of unmatched items and of client document requests. Where a log does not exist, reconstruct the split in a 30-minute interview per book and mark it as reconstructed. The same three books and the same log format are used during the pilot, so the comparison is like-for-like rather than against a firm-wide average. This is an inference on method: the firm has published no close-time data, so the baseline is whatever the firm records.
pilot.exit_criteria: Stop or re-scope if any of these hold: fewer than three QBO books can be identified and granted access (or the only available books need NetSuite/CCH access that cannot be granted inside the pilot window); the reviewer is confirmed to be working in BILL and BILL access cannot be obtained; after two pilot closes, less than 15% reduction in reviewer minutes per book; proposed-entry acceptance below 60%; more than 10% of exceptions needing a second reviewer; any unapproved posting, any reversal for error, or any client-data cross-contamination between books; or the reviewer judges the queue slower than working directly in QuickBooks. If the firm cannot grant write access at all, fall back to a read-only 'exception pack' scope and re-price.

suggested_pricing.pilot_fee: $2,000 for a 4-week pilot on 3 client books (credited in full against the set-up fee if the firm continues) - inference
suggested_pricing.setup_fee: $4,500 one-time for 3 books, including the QBO wiring, the firm's close checklist encoded, the reviewer queue and the first close run; $400 per additional book - inference
suggested_pricing.monthly_fee: $550 per month covering up to 5 books, plus $25 per additional book per month (at 25 books that is $1,050/month, about $42 per book; at 40 books $1,425/month, about $36 per book) - inference
suggested_pricing.reasoning: All figures here are inference, priced against the audit's own impact range and the competitor prices above, not against the firm's (unpublished) billing rate. Year one for the firm on a 5-book engagement is about $11,450 ($2,000 pilot + $4,500 set-up + 9 x $550), against an audit value estimate of $13,600-$43,600 of recovered accountant time - i.e. about 0.84x the low end and about 0.26x the high end. That deliberately leaves the firm most of the upside in the conservative case, because the first reference client is worth more than the margin and because the low-end number is built on unconfirmed volume assumptions. Against the alternatives: a part-time New Jersey clerk is about $35/hour loaded, so 5-10 hours a month of displaced work already covers the monthly fee; Botkeeper would be $447-$596/month for 3-5 licenses at monthly billing ($149 each for 3-4, $109 each at 5), before anyone configures it to the firm's review standard; Double is only $30-$50/month for 3-5 clients on Core ($150-$250 on Scale, plus $500/month if Autoclose is added) but stops at workflow, not reconciliation logic. The $25 per-additional-book step is set so the fee grows with the book without outrunning the value: $42 per book at 25 books sits below Botkeeper's cheapest band ($59 per license/month at 25+) and above Double's $10-$50 per connected client, which reflects that this design does the matching and entry work those tools do not (inference). The $550 base is also small enough to approve against a manager's discretionary budget rather than a capital cycle. If the pilot's measured savings land near the bottom of the audit range, expect to hold at $550 and add books rather than raise the fee; if savings land above $30,000/year, re-price at the renewal to $900-$1,100/month.

leverage.point: Intuit publishes an MIT-licensed QuickBooks Online MCP server with 145 tools, full CRUD on 29 entity types including Journal Entry and Attachable, and QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE/UPDATE/DELETE flags - a large share of the QBO integration work is already written and is permissively reusable.

The QBO API is free at the Builder tier with 500,000 CorePlus credits/month and uncapped Core calls, so the dominant cost of this integration is engineering time, not API fees - a margin a per-seat SaaS product cannot match at small firm scale.

Docling and Langfuse are open source and self-hostable, so the parsing and the audit-trace layer cost nothing in licence fees and stay inside the firm's data boundary - the same two modules are reusable for the tax-season knowledge agent and for the next accounting firm.

Uncat at $9/month/client is a cheap buy for the document-chase slice if the firm prefers not to run that module itself; keeping it as an option lowers the technical risk of the pilot without changing the per-client economics much.

QuickBooks is the one stack fact confirmed from the firm's own site (its QuickBooks accounting service line), so a QBO-only pilot needs no new software on the client side - only OAuth grants. Whether the firm's clients also use Bill.com or NetSuite is unconfirmed and must be established in discovery before it is designed for.

Client documents already arrive through a third-party hosted channel (ProtectedXchange) rather than the firm's own servers, so the design can leave secure storage where it is and add only the request tracking and the QBO attachment step. The channel publishes no API, so intake stays manual.

edge_vs_competitors: Where this design has an edge: (1) integration depth - it is built per client on QuickBooks Online and reads the firm's own checklist, where Double organises the close and Botkeeper standardises to its own workflow; (2) a review-first posting path with an idempotency key, a reversal and a per-line approval record, which is the thing a CPA firm actually has to be able to show; (3) local presence - Edison is roughly ten miles from Milltown, so the founder can sit in the office for a close, tune thresholds with the reviewer in person and be reachable in a way a national SaaS vendor is not; (4) private/US-region deployment with no training on client data, which is directly responsive to the confidentiality and Safeguards rules below and is something the cheapest tools (Uncat at $9/month/client, Double at $10 per connected client) do not sell on; (5) the code is reusable across other multi-client bookkeeping firms, so the second and third sale cost far less to deliver. Where it has no edge, and should not pretend otherwise: no SOC 2 report, no security questionnaire history, no reference clients, no brand, a single founder with no cover during a bad week, and no ability to match Botkeeper's or FloQast's breadth of pre-built features or their support organisation. The honest positioning is 'weeks of engineering plus close attention, at a price a 20-person firm can approve', not 'better than FloQast'.

risks_compliance.issue: Sending client bookkeeping and tax data to a model vendor or any subprocessor can be treated as a disclosure of confidential client information without client consent.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: N.J.A.C. 13:29-3.7(a): a licensee or the licensee's firm shall not, without the client's consent, disclose confidential information obtained in the course of performing professional services.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Add the consultancy as a named service provider in engagement letters or a short consent addendum; keep processing in a US region with no training use; offer a private/on-prem tenancy for clients who will not consent to any external model call; log every disclosure path.

risks_compliance.issue: A CPA firm is a 'financial institution' under the FTC Safeguards Rule, so it must select service providers capable of safeguarding customer information, require safeguards by written contract, and reassess them periodically - the consultancy is exactly that service provider.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: 16 CFR 314.4(f) service-provider oversight (select and retain capable providers; require safeguards by contract; periodically assess).
risks_compliance.mitigation: Sign a written information-security addendum covering encryption, access control, incident notification, subprocessor list and deletion on termination; supply a filled security questionnaire and a network diagram; accept annual reassessment and give the firm audit-log exports.

risks_compliance.issue: Tax preparers must maintain a written information security plan and vet service providers; a vendor touching return information becomes part of that programme.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: IRS Publication 4557 (Rev. 5-2024) - Safeguarding Taxpayer Data; preparers should choose providers capable of protecting taxpayer information, put the safeguards obligation in the contract, and oversee the provider as part of the WISP.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Align the contract with the firm's WISP; document provider vetting before the first book is connected; keep the QBO write path off until the security addendum is signed; provide the firm with the trace logs it needs for its own oversight.

risks_compliance.issue: If any return information (rather than pure bookkeeping data) reaches the system - prior-year figures in a workpaper, a tax export in a close pack - unauthorised use or disclosure carries criminal and civil exposure.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: 26 U.S.C. 7216 makes knowing or reckless unauthorised disclosure or use of return information a misdemeanour, with civil penalties under 6713; 26 CFR 301.7216-2 sets out the permitted disclosures, including to service providers, without consent.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Scope the pilot to bookkeeping entities only, exclude tax returns and return workpapers, and have the firm's counsel confirm the service-provider basis for any return information that does arrive; keep a per-client data map so the firm can see what is in scope.

risks_compliance.issue: The agent can create and post journal entries programmatically, so a wrong or duplicated entry propagates into client financials and, later, into a tax return - a restatement failure mode, not a bad answer.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Intuit's MIT-licensed QuickBooks Online MCP server ships working create/update/delete handlers for the Journal Entry and Attachable entities, so the write path is real and needs controls rather than hoping it is not.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Propose-only by default; approval per line with a named reviewer; dollar and confidence thresholds that force escalation; idempotency keys on posting; one-click reversal; replay a closed month and tie out before the first live posting; QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE=true during ingestion phases.

risks_compliance.issue: Model and vendor data handling: prompts contain client financial data, and default retention or training use would be unacceptable to the firm and its clients.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: OpenAI states that API data is not used to train or improve models as of 1 March 2023 unless the customer opts in, that abuse-monitoring logs are retained up to 30 days by default, that Zero Data Retention is available only to eligible customers subject to prior approval, and that the United States is listed as a region with both regional storage and regional processing (eligibility via sales).
risks_compliance.mitigation: Request Zero Data Retention or modified abuse monitoring approval before the pilot, pin the project to the US region and budget the 10% residency uplift, set store=false, avoid stateful endpoints (threads/vector stores) that are not ZDR-eligible, and keep the option of a self-hosted open-weight model for clients who require it.

risks_compliance.issue: API quota and rate limits can silently break a close run mid-month if the design queries per transaction.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Intuit's App Partner Program Guide: the Builder tier includes 500,000 CorePlus API credits per month and blocks (does not bill) CorePlus calls above the cap, while Core create/update calls are unmetered.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Use batched queries and webhooks rather than per-transaction reads; monitor CorePlus consumption per client per run; keep a cached daily snapshot so a blocked run can still assemble a pack; move to the Silver tier (US$300 per month, 1M CorePlus credits) only if the book grows past the cap.

risks_compliance.issue: Client-facing document-chase email can turn into bulk or repeated messaging, and misconfigured sending damages both deliverability and the firm's reputation.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: No specific rule was confirmed for this design in this revision: it sends no SMS, so TCPA consent questions do not arise, and the reminder caps below are a design choice rather than a regulatory requirement.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Send from the reviewer's own address, cap reminders (for example three over ten days), require reviewer approval of outbound content for the first two weeks, keep a per-client opt-out that the agent respects, and warm the sending domain before the first live chase.

risks_compliance.issue: Unknowns that could change the compliance answer and that this research could not close: the firm's own WISP contents, its client consent language, whether its engagement letters permit third-party processing, and its professional-liability insurer's conditions on AI use.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Could not confirm - no public source exists for the firm's internal policies or its E&O terms.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Ask in discovery and make the security addendum and consent language a condition of the pilot start; if the firm's insurer requires prior notification, the firm files it before any client data is processed.

feasibility.weeks_to_pilot: 6 weeks from signed scope to first live pilot close (about 2 weeks of build before the first close, then 4 weeks covering two monthly closes)
feasibility.reasoning: Technically this is a 3 rather than a 4 or 5: the QBO side is largely solved (Intuit's own MIT-licensed MCP server with Journal Entry and Attachable handlers, a free Builder tier, documented Core/CorePlus split), but the value depends on matching quality across messy client data, on a review UI the firm will actually use, and on safe idempotent posting - and NetSuite and CCH ProSystem remain unproven integration paths. Commercially it is also a 3: the pain is inferred from hiring and site structure rather than from the firm complaining, the client tool stack itself is unconfirmed, the volume assumptions behind the $13,600-$43,600 range are unconfirmed, no client count or billing rate is public, and the decision-maker's name and title are not published on the firm's site - so the first obstacle is finding who signs, not building the thing. Conditions for Go: (1) scope to 3 QuickBooks Online books, read-only first, with BILL added only if discovery confirms it; (2) get the security addendum and consent language agreed before any client data is touched, with US-region processing and ZDR approval requested; (3) make the pilot a measured before/after with a written time-log baseline, and accept that the answer may be 'no saving' for a 5-person book; (4) price at $550/month so the firm's downside is small and the founder gets a reference in a vertical where every other firm has the same problem; (5) do not promise NetSuite, ProSystem or ProtectedXchange automation until those are separately confirmed.

discovery_questions: How many client books do you close each month today, and how many of those are QuickBooks Online versus NetSuite, CCH ProSystem exports or something else?
Do your clients run bills and payments in Bill.com? For how many of the books you would put in a pilot?
Who owns the close for each book now, and who signs off before anything posts - is there a dollar threshold above which a partner looks?
What does your close checklist look like for one representative book, and what does 'done' mean for the pack you send the client?
How many hours does a typical book take from first bank transaction to delivered pack, and do you have any time records we could use as a baseline?
Do you have QuickBooks Online Accountant access to these clients, or would each client need to grant OAuth consent, and who asks them?
What do your engagement letters say about third-party service providers processing client data, and does your E&O insurer have conditions on AI tools?
Do you have a written information security plan (WISP), and who maintains it? Would a vendor security addendum need partner or client sign-off?
Which part of the close would you hand over first if you could hand over only one: the reconciliation exceptions, the client document chase, or the pack assembly?
What is the senior accounting manager hire meant to take off whose plate, and what happens to this work if that hire lands first?
Who else would need to say yes before a paid pilot on three books could start, and what would each of them need to see?
caveats: All impact and pricing figures are inference or the audit's labelled assumptions. The audit's $13,600-$43,600 range rests on 25-40 books a month, 1.5-3 hours per close and a 50% handover rate, none of which the firm has confirmed publicly.

The BLS medians used to value time ($100,830 accountants and auditors, $58,300 bookkeeping clerks, both New Jersey, May 2025) are wage benchmarks, not the firm's billing rates; a CPA firm's billed rate is much higher, so recovered hours are worth more to the firm than the wage figure implies.

Running-cost total is our sum of the sourced lines above: about $57-$107 per month in USD (model $40-90, Postmark Pro $16.50, everything else $0) plus about EUR 11-15 per month of hosting, before any US data-residency uplift on model pricing. No currency conversion is applied because no exchange-rate source was opened.

Botkeeper's per-license prices and Double's tier prices were transcribed from their pricing pages by third-party price indexes because both pages render prices with JavaScript; both were checked in October 2026 and both could change. Verify with the vendor before quoting them to the firm.
FloQast, Numeric, AIwyn-style enterprise close tools and Bookkeeper360's bookkeeping tier publish no price, so the mid-market comparison here is qualitative for those vendors.

The firm's decision-maker is unknown - no owner, managing partner or GM is named on the firm's home, about or contact pages - so the commercial score assumes access can be obtained through the published inbox or a walk-in.

Technical scope is deliberately limited to QuickBooks Online, with BILL conditional. NetSuite and CCH ProSystem clients, ProtectedXchange automation and any tax-season work are excluded from the pilot and priced separately.

No SOC 2, ISO 27001 or pen-test evidence exists for the consultancy at this stage; any firm that runs a security questionnaire will find that out, and the honest answer is 'not yet, here are the controls instead'.
data_gaps: The Senior Accounting Manager job posting body could not be retrieved in this revision (LinkedIn serves it only behind a sign-in/script shell), so the firm's actual client tool list - and specifically whether Bill.com is used by clients - is unverified and is carried as a discovery question.

Botkeeper's own pricing page was opened but its price table is rendered client-side and no figures could be read directly; the $134/$149 per license per month figures come from a third-party price index that states it checked the vendor page on 15 October 2026.

Double's tier prices ($10/$25/$50 per connected client per month) were likewise only readable via a third-party transcription; the vendor page itself yielded the add-on prices only (Autoclose $500/month, Tax Suite $200/month annual commitment, Emails $10/connected team email/month).
Wolters Kluwer's CCH Axcess integration vendor programme page returned HTTP 403, so the existence, terms and cost of a ProSystem/CCH Axcess API route could not be confirmed.
No public API documentation was found for ProtectedXchange, the firm's secure file link, so document intake is treated as a manual hand-off.
The firm publishes no client count, revenue, billing rate, close calendar or hours data, so the baseline for the pilot has to be created from the firm's own time logs.
No public source covers the firm's WISP, engagement-letter consent language or professional-liability insurance conditions on AI tools; these must be asked for in discovery.

Intuit's Builder-tier cap (500,000 CorePlus credits per month) is confirmed, but the actual CorePlus cost of a close run at 25-40 books is our own estimate; it should be measured during the pilot rather than assumed.

Hetzner's cloud page publishes a starting price per tier but no distinct US-region price, and no exchange-rate source was opened, so hosting is quoted in EUR and the US location must be confirmed at sign-up.
